common_name: Marguerite Sweet Potato Vine (Chartreuse-Gold Ornamental Sweet Potato Vine)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants after the last frost in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Marguerite's bright chartreuse-gold foliage color is most vivid in full sun and dims to a softer green in shade.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or container plants in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Marguerite is the classic bright chartreuse-gold companion to the dark-leaved Blackie sweet potato vine, producing large, heart-shaped, glowing yellow-green leaves on fast-growing, trailing vines that quickly spill over the edges of containers, hanging baskets, and garden beds. Its vigorous, weed-smothering growth makes it a popular filler and spiller in mixed plantings, and it tolerates heat, humidity, and drought well once established, needing only occasional trimming to keep it from overwhelming smaller companion plants. Like other ornamental sweet potato vines, it produces edible tuberous roots, though the plant is grown almost exclusively for its foliage rather than as a food crop.

common_name: Big Begonia (Large-Scale Landscape Wax Begonia Series)

planting.note: Plant purchased transplants after last frost in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; the Big series was bred for unusually large, vigorous plants and flowers compared to traditional smaller wax begonias, making a bold impact in beds and large containers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, fertile soil in partial shade to full sun with adequate moisture. The Big begonia series was bred to scale up the classic wax begonia into a much larger, more substantial landscape plant, with glossy leaves and abundant flower clusters in white, pink, or red covering a mounding plant considerably bigger than traditional bedding wax begonias. Its larger size and heat tolerance make it a strong choice for mass plantings, large containers, and borders where a bigger, bolder begonia display is wanted, and it tolerates more direct sun than many begonias provided soil moisture stays consistent. It is largely self-cleaning and needs little maintenance beyond routine watering and fertilizing through the growing season.

common_name: Freida Hemple Caladium (Classic Bright Cherry-Red Fancy-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Freida Hemple is one of the oldest and most famous fancy-leaf caladium cultivars, producing large, heart-shaped leaves in vivid cherry-red centers bordered by a wide, dark green margin, one of the most eye-catching color combinations available among caladiums. Its bold color has made it a mainstay of Southern shade gardens for generations, providing season-long tropical color in beds and containers without the need for flowers. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors over winter in cooler zones ensures better survival.

common_name: Postman Joyner Caladium (Classic Red-and-Green Fancy-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Postman Joyner is a classic fancy-leaf caladium cultivar known for bold, ruffled leaves splashed with bright red centers and prominent dark green veining against a lighter green background, giving strong color contrast in a shaded bed or container planting. It has been a favorite of Southern gardeners for many decades for its reliable performance and vivid color that holds up through a long summer season in the shade garden. In zone 9, tubers can often overwinter in the ground with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing indoors ensures more reliable survival in cooler climates.

common_name: Pink Beauty Caladium (Classic Rose-Pink Fancy-Leaf Caladium)

planting.note: Plant tubers in spring after the last frost when soil has warmed to at least 65 degrees F; plant an inch or two deep in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade.

directions: Plant tubers in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, acidic soil in partial to full shade. Pink Beauty is a long-established fancy-leaf caladium cultivar producing large, heart-shaped leaves in soft rose-pink centers with darker green veining and margins, a gentler, more pastel color combination than the bright reds of many other classic caladium cultivars. It provides months of reliable, low-maintenance color in shaded beds, borders, and containers without needing flowers, pairing especially well with ferns, hostas, and other shade perennials. In zone 9, tubers can often be left in the ground over winter with heavy mulch, though lifting and storing them indoors in cooler climates ensures more reliable survival.
